title: The leper's offering
hook: on his alms round Kassapa stands by a man with leprosy, accepts a lump of rice from his hand, and eats it (Theragatha, Mahakassapa's verses)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhutanga, the strict practices Kassapa kept into old age. Your line: for those to come. Did someone see your one simple practice? Today, one of those alms rounds. Day seven hundred forty-two.

Morning, and an old monk walks down from his lodging into town with his bowl. This is the alms round: you don't choose the food, and you don't choose the giver. You stand, and you receive what's offered. Today the one who wants to give is a man with leprosy, sitting and eating his own meal. Kassapa doesn't cross the street. He goes and stands beside him. And the man lifts a lump of rice in his damaged hand and puts it in the bowl. These lines are Kassapa's own, in the verses the tradition gives him. What he did next is today's story.
screen: `A BOWL, A MORNING ROUND.` → `HE STANDS BESIDE HIM.` → `RICE FROM A DAMAGED HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the offering. In the verses, the man's hand is so damaged by his illness that, as he places the food in the bowl, a finger falls in with it. The poem doesn't look away from that. And Kassapa is standing right beside him. Second, the eating. Kassapa says he sat down by a wall and ate that rice. And he adds the line that gives the story its force: while he was eating, and afterward, he felt no disgust. Third, why he tells it. These aren't boasting verses. They sit among lines about a simple life: food from the alms round, medicine from what others discard, a seat at the foot of a tree. For Kassapa, a gift is a gift. The giver isn't graded first. The man with leprosy got to do what the other householders did. He got to give, and be received. Fourth, what it isn't. The story isn't asking anyone to ignore illness or take risks with health. It's about what comes after a gift is taken: the quiet recoil, the polite thanks and the thing set aside later. The verses say none of that came, not while he ate and not afterward. He didn't only accept it. He ate it. And this closes a week of great disciples: Ananda's tears and his night arahant, the recital, Pippali and Bhadda leaving together, the worn robe, the strict practices, and now a lump of rice from an unexpected hand.
screen: `A GIFT FROM A DAMAGED HAND.` · `HE ATE, AND FELT NO DISGUST.` · `THE GIVER ISN'T GRADED FIRST.` · `NO RECOIL, DURING OR AFTER.` · then, large: `HE ATE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a gift without judging. Settle, and breathe. Think of a gift you accepted politely and then quietly set aside. A clumsy present still in its box. Advice you nodded at and never tried. A dish you praised and didn't finish. Hold that gift in your mind. What was actually offered? What would it take to use it, wear it, try it, the way Kassapa ate the rice? Let yourself receive it fully now. If thanks come up, let them come. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dana, giving. What the man with leprosy offers Kassapa on his alms round, rice from a damaged hand, received and eaten without disgust. Today's word.

Your line: he ate it. Today, when someone offers you something, help, food or advice, don't stop at polite thanks. Use it, taste it, try it, and let the giver see it was received. Day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: On the alms round in Theravada countries, monks walk in silence and receive whatever food is placed in the bowl, from any householder; Kassapa's verses about the leper's rice are one of the texts that show this way of receiving.
